newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU TO RULE ON BELGIAN, FRENCH PLANS TO SAVE JOBS.
newsitem.headline: EU TO RULE ON BELGIAN, FRENCH PLANS TO SAVE JOBS.

text.p: The European Commission is set to clear on Tuesday a Belgian scheme to cut social security charges on manual workers' wages after banning a previous scheme which gave tax breaks to export-led companies only.

The Commission is also expected to announce formally its rejection of French measures to help the textile industry on the same grounds it used in December to overrule the Belgian Maribel scheme -- that sectoral aid schemes distort fair competition in the EU's single market.

On March 12, the Commission found the French textile scheme, in force since July 1996, unacceptable because it would transfer unemployment problems to other regions in the EU. But it delayed a decision to give France time to revise the rules.

Commission sources said they had not received any precise new plan from the French authorities but it had been told the French intended extending the rules to labour-intensive sectors and particularly manual workers.
"If they extend it to all sectors, putting the accent on manual workers, we will look into it sympathetically," a Commission official said on Monday.
That, however, would not prevent a negative decision on the existing scheme, named after French Industry Minister Franck Borotra, the source said.
The Borotra plan was expected to save firms 2.1 billion French francs in social security contributions over two years.

The Commission's decision will not affect 11,300 small and medium-sized firms, of the 13,000 companies set to benefit from the scheme, provided that the aid involved does not exceed 100,000 European currency units per SME over three years.

In December, the Commission asked Belgium to reclaim 11.4 billion Belgian francs in salary-linked tax breaks that exporting firms should have paid in 1995. This came after the Belgian authorities only agreed cosmetic changes to the Maribel scheme.

The new scheme -- called Maribel four -- will allow all Belgian companies to save between 20,000 and 33,000 Belgian francs in social security charges per year per worker, depending on the proportion of manual workers in the total workforce.
The Belgian authorities have excluded financial services and the energy sector from Maribel because of the low percentage of manual workers they employ.
Companies with five workers or less will be able to reduce contributions by a flat 34,000 Belgian francs a year per worker.
"We appreciate this is positive for manual work and moreover it is a general, not sectoral, measure," the Commission official said.

The Commission has made it crystal clear that it will not tolerate sectoral aid schemes even if motivated by the intention to preserve or create jobs. It has called instead for an overall reduction in non-wage labour costs to help reduce the bloc's huge unemployment.
